How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • Recent findings suggest that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

Recent findings suggest that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

In a recent development, no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful fresh AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella noted, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

Industry observers note that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

In a recent development, MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a organization partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in significant, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the organization with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

It has been revealed that most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from upcoming finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

According to recent reports, since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

Sources indicate that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

In a recent development, microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple people to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to problem OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

Industry observers note that OOBs are notable enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security problem involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Recent findings suggest that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he remarked, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

Industry observers note that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

Sources indicate that it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

Industry News: Billionaire Frank Slootman gives 22,081 Montana kids $1,000 each for their Trump Accounts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, are giving more than $22 million to children in their home state of Montana.
  • The gift covers 22,081 children, totaling $22,081,000.
  • Recent findings suggest that those children were born too early for the federal government’s own $1,000 deposit, which goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, are giving more than $22 million to children in their home state of Montana. The couple is putting $1,000 into the Trump Account of every Montana child born in 2023 or 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department announced on Nov. 19.

The gift covers 22,081 children, totaling $22,081,000. The Slootman Family Foundation stated the money has already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children’s accounts, according to NBC Montana.

Recent findings suggest that those children were born too early for the federal government’s own $1,000 deposit, which goes only to children born from 2025 through 2028. The Slootmans’ gift gives them the same start. At $1,000 a child, it is also four times the per-child amount in Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion national pledge.

Recent findings suggest that “Montana is the Last Best Place,” the Slootmans said in a statement. “We want to give Montana children an even faster start in life. The money in your account is yours, it cannot be accessed by anybody, not even by you until you are at least 18 years old. What you can do is watch it grow, ask for contributions on birthdays, holidays, and other special occasions to make your account compound in value even more.”.

According to recent reports, gov. Greg Gianforte thanked the family for what he called “this significant investment.”.

Industry observers note that frank Slootman, Snowflake’s chairman and former CEO, led the cloud data firm through its 2020 initial public offering after taking two other technology companies, Data Domain and ServiceNow, public. Bloomberg Law reported that the Bloomberg Billionaires Index put his net worth at $3.1 billion when the gift was revealed.

It has been revealed that slootman, born in the Netherlands, has lived in Bozeman for years. When Snowflake eliminated its corporate headquarters in 2021, it named its Bozeman office its principal executive office because Slootman and the tech giant’s CFO lived in the city, Fortune reported at the time.

The family foundation has given to Montana causes before, including $1 million to American Prairie Foundation, a conservation group assembling a large prairie reserve in the state, in 2022 and $1.5 million in each of the next two years, according to its tax filings. This latest gift is on another scale: It roughly matches the $22.7 million in net assets the foundation reported at the end of 2024, the latest year for which its filings are public.

Slootman has also backed Montana Republicans. While he was ServiceNow’s CEO, he gave the maximum allowed contribution to Gianforte, then the state’s congressman, CNBC reported in 2021. Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, publicly thanked the couple for the gift last week, calling it “an incredible bet on Montana’s future.”.

Industry observers note that created under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax law, a Trump Account is a type of individual retirement account for children. Parents, relatives, and employers can contribute, generally up to a combined $5,000 a year during childhood. Contributions from charities to a broad group of children, such as every child born in a state in a given year, don’t count toward that cap.

Recent findings suggest that the money goes into low-cost funds that track broad U.S. stock indexes, such as the S&P 500, so its value rises or falls with the market. Investment earnings generally aren’t taxed until you withdraw the money.

Recent findings suggest that families generally can’t withdraw the money until the calendar year the child turns 18. After that, traditional IRA rules apply, and withdrawals can trigger taxes and early withdrawal penalties.

In a recent development, the Treasury Department has opened accounts for eligible children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Nearly 70 million children now have one, a White House spokesman told Fortune this month. Only U.S. citizens born from Jan. 1, 2025, through Dec. 31, 2028, qualify for the government’s one-time $1,000 deposit.

Industry observers note that some Montana children covered by the Slootmans’ gift may have already received $250 from Michael and Susan Dell. The Dells’ gift reached 25 million children born from 2016 through 2024, starting in zip codes with the lowest median family incomes. The Slootmans’ announcement mentioned 118,523 Montana children are eligible for the Dells’ $250.

A Montana child who qualified for both gifts would have $1,250 from the two couples.

Recent findings suggest that parents can claim their child’s account through the official Trump Accounts app by verifying their identity and their relationship to the child. Once an account is claimed, relatives can add their own contributions. Fortune has a guide to who gets the $1,000 and how to claim an account.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous financial educator and author of "Rich Dad Poor Dad" Robert Kiyosaki has disclosed when investors should begin accumulating Bitcoin (BTC) during the current cryptocurrency market bloodbath.

While he is consistently bullish on Bitcoin, Kiyosaki is asking investors to be patient and not buy the flagship cryptocurrency before the current crash ends.

Recent findings suggest that in his latest X post on Nov. 20, Kiyosaki shared an notable investment lesson and warned his followers against catching a falling knife.

"Never grab a falling knife," Kiyosaki warned.

The financial guru suggested that this means investors should wait until the cryptocurrency market crash ends before buying more Bitcoin.

"That means wait for the crash to end….before buying," Kiyosaki elaborated.

Notably, Kiyosaki shared that he began buying Bitcoin when its price was around $20,000 after another major market crash.

The best-selling author hinted that he is planning to do the same during the current market downturn.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," Kiyosaki noted.

The financial educator reminded his followers of one of his important investment tips.

"Your profit is made when you buy….not when you sell," Kiyosaki noted.

Basically, the financial educator suggested that investors should prioritize finding good entry prices rather than trying to buy Bitcoin while its price keeps dropping.

However, Kiyosaki did not specify a Bitcoin price target or how he is going to know that the market has bottomed out.

Kiyosaki's remarks follow another devastating Bitcoin crash that took the flagship cryptocurrency to its lowest level in more than four months.

In a recent development, on Nov. 20, the world's largest cryptocurrency crashed below the key psychological price level of $60,000 for the first time since July.

According to Reuters, Bitcoin crashed to around $59,381. Bitcoin shed over 3% in a single trading session.

Interestingly, BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) saw a record $541.1 million in daily outflows.

Industry observers note that overall, the latest data shows that November has seen total net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs worth around $3.47 billion.

Interestingly, Kiyosaki has shared his excitement about buying Bitcoin during major market corrections several times.

According to recent reports, earlier, on Nov. 20, Kiyosaki described the ongoing market crash as a possible buying opportunity. He suggested that experienced investors are sitting back and waiting to accumulate while bad investors are trying to sell everything.

It has been revealed that "I am most excited about Bitcoin's crash. Waiting to buy more," Kiyosaki declared.

In a recent development, kiyosaki stressed that Bitcoin has a limited supply of 21 million coins. He believes that this scarcity makes Bitcoin vastly different from traditional government-issued currencies.

Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night?
  • But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Recent findings suggest that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla mentioned. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

In a recent development, gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

According to recent reports, if you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

Industry observers note that the platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for people.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

In a recent development, birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

It has been revealed that the impossible research burden on newly introduced parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

In a recent development, how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — substantial metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your tech giant?

It has been revealed that it’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Industry observers note that turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

According to recent reports, earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our firm has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#87565. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally.
  • Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance.
  • I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:27 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure tech giant with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:.

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

Recent findings suggest that HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers remarked networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around significant platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

It has been revealed that many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

Sources indicate that “I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he remarked. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he remarked. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”.

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Sources indicate that evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

According to recent reports, the second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math indicates Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

Sources indicate that the back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

It has been revealed that for old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Industry observers note that fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Valuable Records are Available for Free Online.

SILVER SPRING, Md. , Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Genealogical Society (NGS) is excited to share that the Preserve the Pensions project to digitize War of 1812 pension files is finished, and the files are now available to the public for free permanently with full-text search via Fold3.

The culmination of sixteen years of fundraising and careful work to save deteriorating files and make them accessible online, this project provides genealogists and family historians with nearly three million pages of records from approximately 90,000 individual files. A partnership between NGS, Fold3, Ancestry, FamilySearch, and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and contributions from people and organizations across the genealogy community, made this incredible endeavor possible and illustrate the power of collaboration.

According to recent reports, "After successfully raising the $2.7 million needed to conserve and digitize the War of 1812 pensions deposited with NARA in Washington, DC, we are thrilled that our digitization partner, Fold3, has completed digitizing the last box of pensions. This effort, originally initiated as a request from the National Archives, concludes the largest private/public partnership the genealogical community has had where donations led directly to making these invaluable records freely available," remarked NGS President David E. Rencher, AG, CG, FUGA, FIGRS, FNGS, FSG. "We thank all who have donated to the project and to those of our partners and the many genealogical societies who spearheaded efforts to raise the funds needed, particularly the Indiana, Illinois, and Fairfax, Virginia, Genealogical Societies.".

Sources indicate that war of 1812 pensions provide information on a generation between the Revolutionary War and the 1850 census, which is the first census to provide the names of individuals in a household. The files may include an affidavit from the soldier or widow including where he enlisted, where he served, and for how long. The widow may state their date of marriage, when he died, a Bible record which may include the names and birth dates of children, and affidavits from other relatives which may help prove family relationships. Sometimes the information about the widow or an affidavit from her will disclose her maiden name. These files may also contain other meaningful military records and information on a person's fellow veterans or neighbors.

According to recent reports, "These records are extremely valuable to researchers and historians, and we are proud to be a part of this project. We're grateful for the efforts started by the Federation of Genealogical Societies before it merged with NGS in 2020, and it has been an honor to carry this forward and continue the work with our partners to see it to completion," said NGS Executive Director Matt Menashes, CAE.

Industry observers note that "The project serves as a template for future initiatives illustrating that together, the genealogical community can help preserve and make available important genealogical records for generations to come. These records may be used not only for genealogy, but also for those studying history and as part of a school curriculum for students," stated Rencher. "Thank you to all who made this possible!".

Sources indicate that NGS offers an online course, War of 1812 Records, for anyone wanting a deeper understanding of how to interpret these records and what other records might add to the story. The modules guide participants through War of 1812 military records, historical context, and research strategies. More information and registration can be found on the NGS website.

Access the War of 1812 pension files via Fold3 and learn more about the project's completion on their blog.

SOURCE National Genealogical Society.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sometimes the best investments are more about a gut feeling than hard numbers.
  • Sources indicate that in 1995, a mere two years before Amazon would go public, and more than 30 years  before it would surpass Walmart to clinch the No.
  • Sources indicate that according to a 1997 prospectus, his mother Jacklyn Gise Bezos, who died in 2025, and stepfather Miguel “Mike” Bezos, gave their son $245,573 from their savings so he could get his business off the ground.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sometimes the best investments are more about a gut feeling than hard numbers. At least that holds true for Jeff Bezos’ parents, who bet on their son when few others would.

Sources indicate that in 1995, a mere two years before Amazon would go public, and more than 30 years  before it would surpass Walmart to clinch the No. 1 spot on the Fortune 500, Bezos received a lifeline from his parents.

Sources indicate that according to a 1997 prospectus, his mother Jacklyn Gise Bezos, who died in 2025, and stepfather Miguel “Mike” Bezos, gave their son $245,573 from their savings so he could get his business off the ground. The six-figure sum represented a “large fraction” of their life savings at the time, according to Bezos, but it would eventually make them both billionaires.

Yet, before he accepted his parents’ money, Bezos made it abundantly clear to them that they might never get it back.

“I want you to know how risky this is,” Mike Bezos recalled his son saying in a 2015 interview. “Because I want to come home at dinner for Thanksgiving and I don’t want you to be mad at me.”.

Bezos put the odds that his online bookseller would succeed at about 30%, which he previously remarked was generous given that the overall success rate for startups is closer to 10%.

A year before his parents invested, Bezos had approached 60 investors asking for $50,000 minimum investments as he sought to reach $1 million in funding. Only 22 of the people he approached agreed to invest, including his parents and two younger siblings, Mark and Christina Bezos Poore.

Still, in the end, his parents made the investment despite the long odds—and despite his stepfather’s first question about the company being “What’s the internet,” Bezos joked.

Recent findings suggest that “He wasn’t making a bet on this tech giant or this concept,” Bezos said of his stepfather in an interview with the Academy of Achievement. “He was making a bet on his son, as was my mother.”.

Almost immediately after opening Amazon’s online store in 1995, Bezos told the Academy of Achievement he was surprised to see orders coming in from all 50 states and from 45 different countries.

Recent findings suggest that at that time, the firm had about 10 employees. By 1997, the company had grown to more than 600. It went public that year at $18 per share, and raised $54 million. Bezos became a billionaire by 1998 thanks to his 40% stake in Amazon, and today,  he holds the title of the world’s third richest person, with a net worth of $283 billion, per the Bloomberg Billionaire Index.

Sources indicate that as for Bezos’ parents, their initial bet on their son turned out to be one of the most successful venture investments of all time. It’s unclear how many shares Mike Bezos has in his possession after his wife died last year, but the couple donated 595,027 shares to the Bezos Family Foundation from 2001 through 2016.

If Mike Bezos still retained the rest of their original 1.4 million shares, they would be worth an estimated $51.7 billion at today’s stock price, according to Fortune’s calculations. Bezos’ siblings Mark and Christina, who each invested $10,000 in Amazon in 1996, according to the prospectus, would also each have shares worth more than $1 billion today if they had never sold any.

Industry observers note that amazon’s shares have skyrocketed more than 208,000% since its IPO in 1997. And just last month, the manufacturer’s shares hit their all-time-high stock price of $287 per share.

The Bezos family later turned some of the wealth they got from Amazon toward philanthropy. In 2000, Mike and Jackie founded the Bezos Family Foundation with their three children—Jeff, Mark and Christina—and their spouses. Since then, the foundation has focused largely on education and child development, funding research and programs aimed at helping young people from birth through high school.

“We were fortunate enough that we have lived overseas and we have saved a few pennies so we were able to be an angel investor,” Mike noted of him and his wife’s initial Amazon investment. “The rest is history.”.

In a recent development, bitcoin saw $554.28 million in liquidations, and 91.3% of that amount came from long positions. Ethereum (ETH) fell below $1,700 on Nov. 20, and ETH traders saw $331.08 million in liquidations. Binance accounted for 45.8% of all liquidations, and the largest single order was also on Binance: an $11.98 million ETHUSDT long position that was liquidated at $1,638.78.

XRP saw $14.67 million in liquidations, and $13.86 million of that amount came from long positions.

Sources indicate that stock markets fell on the same day. The Nasdaq Composite has given back all of its gains for 2026, and the S&P 500 fell 1.82% to 7,045.5 points. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones are now down 10% from their record highs. The VIX volatility index jumped 8.09% to 30.73.

Nvidia has lost $2.55 trillion in market value since its Oct. 6 peak. Anthropic shares started trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19. On Nov. 20, the stock fell about 10% in premarket trading, and it was close to its IPO price of $83.

Nvidia futures on crypto exchanges saw $26.79 million in liquidations, according to CoinGlass. Anthropic contracts saw $15.29 million in liquidations, and 90.7% of that amount came from long positions.

Microsoft ‘To Do’ customers make a major to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal owners that Microsoft To Do would be their fresh home.
  • Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.

According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal owners that Microsoft To Do would be their fresh home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

Sources indicate that the reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft claims Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

It has been revealed that why Microsoft is doing it: The company remarked putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A newly introduced Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday customers, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

In a recent development, rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent manufacturer, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist customers may end up back with the people who built it.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano-linked privacy blockchain Midnight has inked a significant initial deal with a Japanese payments company as it aims to make further inroads into traditional finance.
  • The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.
  • 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed noted the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano-linked privacy blockchain Midnight has inked a significant initial deal with a Japanese payments company as it aims to make further inroads into traditional finance.

The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.

Per a Nov. 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed noted the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments firm.

Recent findings suggest that syed did not name the company. But the deal is a substantial one for Midnight’s bid to establish a presence in Japan’s financial services sector.

However, it is just an initial agreement, and no commercial services have been rolled out in Japan yet.

It is also worth noting that the Midnight Foundation is talking to some major Japanese banks and companies working with intellectual property and medical data.

According to Syed, he spent two days in Tokyo meeting with major financial institutions and other companies.

Japan has been a key market for Midnight, along with the United States.

According to Midnight Foundation Japan country manager Taro Kimura, Japan is the only Asian country where the foundation has a local representative on the ground.

Midnight has been eyeing Japan more keenly due to the country’s sizeable Cardano community.

The Japanese push comes hot on the heels of a historic development in the British banking sector.

On Nov. 18, British financial institution Monument Bank started tokenizing retail customer deposits on Midnight. It is the first UK bank to launch such a product on a public blockchain.

It has been revealed that the first phase of the venture involves up to £250 million in tokenized deposits. For this, the bank is offering customers a 12-month fixed annual interest rate of 5.2%.

According to recent reports, midnight employs zero-knowledge cryptography to safeguard sensitive transaction details, unlike traditional public blockchains. As a result, banks can meet compliance requirements while keeping their customers’ private information and transaction details out of public view.

#87557. Billionaire Fanatics CEO made millions as a teenager but nearly lost it all by 16: ‘Each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success’

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (831 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Billionaire Fanatics CEO made millions as a teenager but nearly lost it all by 16: ‘Each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes.
  • For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.
  • Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes. But the company has grown into a powerhouse in its own right, striking partnerships with nearly every major U.S. sports league, including the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and generating roughly $14 billion in annual revenue.

For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business. By 13, he was selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania, and a year later, he had opened his own storefront just down the road from his home. He was making money quickly—and even joined up with a friend to buy a Porsche before he could legally drive.

But around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, so his customers weren’t coming.

It has been revealed that “It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled in a recent conversation with podcaster David Senra. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”.

In a recent development, to get himself out of the hole, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, went door to door borrowing money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a upcoming venture in the closeout business to repay his loan within three weeks. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales, buying and selling closeout merchandise.

In a recent development, “I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt; thought I was a complete failure, giving up on entrepreneurship—to five years later, doing $150 million, making $10 million to $15 million a year as a kid,” Rubin said. “And so to me, each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success.”.

According to recent reports, rubin spent just one semester at Villanova University before dropping out to focus on business. He continued building his sports merchandise operation, KPR Sports, which eventually became part of Global Sports Inc., later renamed GSI Commerce.

As the internet took off, Rubin shifted the business toward e-commerce, helping major retailers and sports teams sell merchandise online.

Sources indicate that but the 2008 financial crisis nearly wiped him out again. Rubin had borrowed heavily against his GSI stock, which lost roughly 90% of its value during the bear market. He began calling a friend who managed a hedge fund, where Rubin had invested $5 million, repeatedly asking for his money back. After roughly 100 calls, he finally got it—with just hours to spare before the bank could seize his shares.

The business eventually rebounded and was bought by eBay in 2011 for $2.4 billion. As part of the deal, Rubin bought back the manufacturer’s sports e-commerce business, laying the foundation for today’s Fanatics.

The firm has since grown into a giant valued at $31 billion in 2022, while Rubin’s personal fortune has grown to an estimated $11.6 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Still, Rubin stated he wouldn’t trade the ups and downs that got him to his level of success today.

“I liked the adrenaline of fighting for my life,” Rubin said.

“If it’s the same s–t every day, it’s boring,” he added. “Business is a roller coaster. Business is an adventure. If you’re a real entrepreneur, you like that. You thrive on that.”.

Fortune reached out to Fanatics for further comment.

Rubin isn’t the only successful business leader to have nearly lost it all at a young age.

In the early days of Ray Dalio building out his now-multibillion-dollar hedge fund business, he was broke, living in Fresh York City—and had to ask his father to borrow $4,000 to help cover bills.

The experience gave him humility, but also made him develop a deep respect for those who do fail—and embrace the lessons learned.

“Anyone you see succeeding is only succeeding at the things you’re paying attention to—I guarantee they are also failing at lots of other things,” Dalio wrote.

“The people I respect most are those who fail well. I respect them even more than those who succeed. That is because failing is a painful experience, while succeeding is a joyous one, so it requires much more character to fail, change, and then succeed than to just succeed.”.

Industry observers note that mark Cuban has echoed that failure is an inevitable part of building a successful career. On his path to a $9.8 billion net worth, he made countless early missteps—from trying to sell powdered milk to getting fired from jobs to making bad investments. The ability to not let these missteps define your entire career is what matters.

Industry observers note that “No one is going to know or care about your failures, and neither should you,”  he mentioned. “All you have to do is learn from them.”.

  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the manufacturer acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the manufacturer’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company claims it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows patch used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

It has been revealed that the final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report indicates.

In a recent development, first, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Sources indicate that second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

In a recent development, third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

Recent findings suggest that how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report states.

Recent findings suggest that the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It has been revealed that it also looks to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

It has been revealed that some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it looks to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it notes. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

In a recent development, the new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the manufacturer indicates, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, iraq has turned down OPEC+'s commissioned review of how much oil it can produce, according to Bloomberg. The dispute could spark a confrontation at the group's online meeting on Sunday, Nov 29., where OPEC and its allies, under Saudi leadership, initiative to rely on the findings to set production targets.

Baghdad is contesting a study by outside consultants, who put its maximum capacity at less than 5 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg. Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair has written to OPEC to insist that Iraq can reach 5.2 million barrels a day.

Sources indicate that under the review, a country given a bigger capacity figure has a firmer basis for seeking a larger output allowance, according to Bloomberg. Iraq's oil ministry and OPEC's secretariat in Vienna had not responded to requests for comment from Bloomberg as of its publication.

This year, Iraq warned it could exit OPEC unless the assessment credited it with a sufficiently large number, according to Bloomberg. Iraq later withdrew the warning. The warning came weeks after the United Arab Emirates' exit from the group, and the UAE has since pushed its production to record levels.

Iraq has bristled at OPEC+ quotas for 10 years, wanting to boost its earnings and restore an economy hurt by war and sanctions, according to Bloomberg.

Industry observers note that the two sides have also differed on how much Iraq is producing. Iraq told OPEC its October output came to nearly 4.9 million barrels daily, the highest of the wartime period and far over its quota, according to Bloomberg. Figures that OPEC draws from outside sources put the number at 4.491 million barrels a day.

OPEC and its allies have been examining the volumes each member can technically produce as groundwork for 2027 output targets.

According to recent reports, separately, the International Energy Agency put Iraq's sustainable capacity at 4.87 million barrels a day in its monthly oil market report this month. The agency estimated Iraq's October output at 4.6 million barrels a day, the highest since September 2019.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are criticizing Nvidia Corp.’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

Sources indicate that the criticism came against the backdrop of a controversial move by the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency applied fresh export restrictions to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud operator. The tech giant played a prominent role in the spy controversy that led to Huang’s resignation. According to trade experts, the Commerce Department left out a key clause that is usually included in such restrictions.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Early reporting about the relationship indicated that she was found to have passed intelligence to China. The U.S. Justice Department later stated that it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang is a spy. Earlier this week, the Upcoming York Times reported that she maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence official.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and tech industry figures urged directors to bring him back. The move drew widespread criticism from members of Congress.

According to recent reports, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-Latest York), who is set to become House Speaker, called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), the chair of House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies and Innovation, remarked that “it’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO.” Former Utah Republican Senator and Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney tweeted: “Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse.”.

Sources indicate that multiple lawmakers told CNBC that they plan to scrutinize Huang’s conduct closely. The executive is scheduled to testify before multiple Congressional committees next Tuesday. Furthermore, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) told the outlet that Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s role in the matter.

Sources indicate that the Commerce Department today added Megaspeed and several of its regional affiliates to its Entity List. Companies on the list can only purchase sensitive products such as graphics cards if they obtain a license from the U.S. government. According to Gizmodo, the move has drawn scrutiny because the restrictions applied to Megaspeed include a loophole.

All the companies on the Entity List are prohibited from buying Nvidia’s latest chips unless they secure a license. Most of them are also unable to buy lower-end graphics cards, high-bandwidth memory and related hardware. The latter restrictions are specified in a clause called the FDPR provision. The Commerce Department has reportedly not applied the FDPR provision to Megaspeed when it added the organization to the Entity List.

In a recent development, huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters on Monday. The news sent the chipmaker’s stock soaring more than 30%, although it parred some of the gains today. Nvidia shares are down 5.8% from Monday.

Sources indicate that wired today published excerpts from Huang’s all-hands meeting with employees. The executive apologized for his affairs and for his management style, which has also come under scrutiny in recent days. He added that he will undergo a “360-degree review” and that Nvidia’s code of conduct is still in effect.
