#87550. Tech Report: Nvidia degrades U.S. national security as Chinese military snags its chips

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2021 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Nvidia degrades U.S. national security as Chinese military snags its chips

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Super Micro compliance auditors visited a Southeast Asian customer in August 2025 to inspect thousands of servers packed with Nvidia chips, the warehouse floor looked in order.
  • According to recent reports, fifteen months later, the country is once again being asked to take tidy paperwork at face value.
  • Recent findings suggest that official endorsements cannot wish away the serious security record piling up in the public view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Super Micro compliance auditors visited a Southeast Asian customer in August 2025 to inspect thousands of servers packed with Nvidia chips, the warehouse floor looked in order. According to federal prosecutors, the scene was pure theater. The servers on hand were nonworking dummies staged for the audit; the real ones had already gone to China. When Commerce Department inspectors came later, conspirators set up the same fakes again, using a hair dryer to swap labels and serial stickers. Prosecutors say at least $510 million in servers went to China over a few weeks in spring 2025 alone.

According to recent reports, fifteen months later, the country is once again being asked to take tidy paperwork at face value. In less than two weeks, Nvidia’s leadership turmoil swung through an astonishing reversal. Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on November 12, and five days later the company’s chairman declared that the board “does not intend to reinstate” him. Come Monday, directors brought him back anyway, citing assurances from senior U.S. officials and concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump claimed credit for talking them into it, telling CNBC, “It’s a threat to lose him.”.

Recent findings suggest that official endorsements cannot wish away the serious security record piling up in the public view. Set aside, for a moment, the scrutiny swirling around Megaspeed, the firm tied to Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, as well as the question of whether she acted as a spy. Even apart from that controversy, a largely overlooked trove of documentation proves beyond dispute that restricted and banned Nvidia chips have been illegally shipped into China, where the Chinese military has openly recorded buying elite processors to bolster capabilities aimed against the United States.

Recent findings suggest that congressional investigators, state attorneys general, and the broader national security community will inevitably unravel what transpired with Megaspeed and Alice Huang. As they pursue that thread, however, they cannot lose sight of the larger pipeline operating right under Washington’s nose. Smuggled American chips are already strengthening the Chinese Communist Party’s military power and domestic repression, fueling weapons research, design, and manufacturing alongside electronic warfare and intelligence collection. Before anyone treats Huang’s return as case closed, investigators must confront the pressing, unanswered questions still hanging over Nvidia.

Consider some of the military-linked recipients already plainly visible in public records. A Reuters investigation published November 11 found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, a military-linked institution on the U.S. export blacklist since 2001 over alleged missile proliferation, recorded an October purchase of two H200 chips through a Chinese supplier. Its cybersecurity school also contracted in January for access to two servers containing eight H200s apiece.

Some advocates point out that the H200 is an older and less sensitive chip, but the administration’s January H200 licensing relaxation explicitly did not erase restrictions on blacklisted entities. Indeed, its safeguards expressly excluded military and military-intelligence owners and prohibited remote access for specified restricted parties. The university’s disturbing procurement records therefore demand a detailed explanation: what authorization, if any, covered these supplies, and which intermediary checked the actual beneficiary? Did the U.S. government authorize these sales (it would be ludicrously stupid if so), or did Nvidia fail in its responsibility to monitor its own supply chain and maintain awareness of end customers?

The Harbin Institute of Technology offers another disturbing example. When Commerce blacklisted it in 2020, the department specifically cited efforts to acquire American technology for Chinese missile programs. Yet Reuters reported this March that Harbin’s July 2025 procurement notice described a Super Micro system containing eight Nvidia A100s. Beihang University, another blacklisted institution with military ties, recorded purchasing a workstation with four A100s in March 2026.

Sources indicate that at a minimum, all of this points to persistent demand from the Chinese military and institutions linked to it — the very institutions the controls were designed to exclude and the very institutions that want to hurt U.S. national security the most. Who is dropping the ball here?

According to recent reports, if the Chinese military has its way, more banned Nvidia chips will soon be on their way. WireScreen reviewed more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records. The units seeking Nvidia hardware include the Rocket Force, which operates China’s land-based nuclear missiles, the Cyberspace Force, and the equipment arm of the Communist Party’s Central Military Commission. One Cyberspace Force tender for A100-class servers named a password-cracking tool as the workload. Georgetown researchers found a PLA lab requesting 16 H100s and another unit seeking a DeepSeek-linked cyber range for “intelligent attack.”  That should scare any and every American.

It is not just the Chinese military obtaining older, still-restricted Nvidia chips. There is also ample evidence that the most cutting-edge, most sensitive chips—such as the Blackwell chip, which is entirely banned from being sold into China—are still making their way into China anyway, and worse, directly into the hands of the CCP. Last month, the AI security firm Lava reported finding 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs operating on Chinese networks—specifically linked to state-owned China Telecom—during a study of more than 12,000 GPUs, despite a ban on Blackwell chips going to China. That comes on top of the fact that even a senior administration official notes DeepSeek trained a model on banned Blackwell chips, likely in Inner Mongolia. Congressional investigators should demand answers about how these Blackwell chips are getting into China and whether Nvidia is asleep at the switch on the most basic KYC duties—know your customer.

Nvidia surely must know about the transshipment of its sensitive chips into China – as has already been proven in the public record, with a long trail of criminal indictments. Alan Hao Hsu and his company, Hao Global, pleaded guilty in October 2025. According to the Justice Department, the scheme involved at least $160 million in exported and attempted exports of restricted Nvidia H100 and H200 processors. Shipping documents concealed the goods and recipients; more than $50 million in funding originated in China. The company’s plea agreement identifies transshipment through Singapore and Malaysia. This is admitted criminal conduct involving falsified documentation and illegal exports through transshipments, yet what did Nvidia do about the facilitators of that transshipment who were still getting chips from Nvidia?

Similarly, in March, federal prosecutors alleged that defendants connected to Super Micro arranged purchases through a Southeast Asian intermediary and diverted at least $510 million in servers to China within weeks in spring 2025, then used the dummy servers described at the outset to cover their tracks. In October, broker Ting-Wei Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including export-control conspiracy and obstruction. Similarly, Taiwan has indicted a senior Nvidia manager as the central figure in faking a compliance audit so that 74 servers of top-line B300 chips could reach China. Given these apparent leaks and holes across Nvidia’s supply chain, any reasonable observer would conclude the organization needs to monitor its own customers and employees far more carefully.

Whenever Washington weighs a firmer line on chips, the same warning reliably surfaces. Push Beijing too hard, skeptics caution, and China will choke off the rare earth magnets powering everything from fighter jets to electric motors. That anxiety is already dictating policy. After the administration let Nvidia resume H20 sales to China last year, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was candid about the bargain, explaining, “We put that in the trade deal with the magnets.” Export controls once considered untouchable have stayed on the bargaining table ever since.

Beijing’s current leverage is undeniable. According to the International Energy Agency, China mines roughly 60% of the world’s magnet rare earths, refines around 90%, and makes nearly 95% of finished permanent magnets. Its grip tightens further on heavy rare earths like dysprosium and terbium, which keep magnets working at high temperatures inside military hardware and electric vehicle motors. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence found that as recently as 2024, the West depended on China for 99% of those heavy minerals. Nor has Beijing hesitated to flex that advantage. Export controls imposed in April 2025 on seven heavy rare earths remain in force. In June, China blacklisted two American firms championed by federal policymakers, MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, and this month it extended a pause on broader restrictions by just two months.

In a recent development, their dominance, however, is a product of policy rather than geology, and it can erode far faster than conventional wisdom expects. Rare earths are not actually rare. All 17 occur outside China, and the U.S. Geological Survey estimates that more than 40 percent of reported global reserves—and an even larger share of identified deposits—lie beyond China’s borders, including 11 million metric tons in Brazil alone, along with major deposits across Australia, Canada, Greenland, Tanzania, and the United States. As late as the 1980s, the world’s leading producer was not in Asia at all, but a single mine in California’s Mojave Desert called Mountain Pass. China assembled its commanding lead in roughly twenty years.

Sources indicate that japan has already demonstrated how swiftly the balance can shift. After Beijing halted exports to Japan in 2010, Tokyo bankrolled Australia’s Lynas and cut China’s share of Japanese rare earth imports from over 90% to roughly 60% within a decade. Lynas has since become the first producer outside China capable of separating both dysprosium and terbium.

The true bottleneck is not ore, but processing capacity and permits, both of which can be solved in years instead of decades. While the IEA estimates that meeting demand for magnet rare earths outside China will require roughly $60 billion over the next ten years, the figure is a modest fraction of the $1.2 trillion in U.S. economic activity Bloomberg calculates depends on these materials. Washington has begun laying the groundwork, pairing a Pentagon stake and price floor for MP Materials with the $12 billion Project Vault stockpile and $565 million for Brazil’s Serra Verde, which supplies those same vital heavy rare earths.

Recent findings suggest that permitting remains the stubborn obstacle. S&P Global calculates that taking a upcoming American mine from discovery to production averages 29 years, slower than every country on earth except Zambia and almost ten years behind Australia. Delays on such a scale turn responsible oversight into outright paralysis. Clearing the logjam demands an “Operation Warp Speed” for critical minerals, built on hard permitting deadlines, one lead agency per project, guaranteed offtake for allied producers stretching from Brazil and Canada to Africa, and strict environmental standards enforced upfront without endless litigation. Smart environmental policy is essential, yet reflexive obstruction simply ships both the mining and the pollution straight to China.

Beijing’s rare earth card is a wasting asset, provided Washington chooses to make it one. The answer is to build, not to bend, and certainly not to keep weakening the export controls standing between America’s best technology and the People’s Liberation Army.

Congress holds subpoena power, and they ought to wield it to get to the bottom of how the Chinese military is obtaining banned Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s shipment ledger for every GPU sent to Southeast Asia since October 2022 is fair game and in the organization’s possession, as are any location data its fleet-management software has collected, its customer files and communication with US regulators, including the Department of Commerce.

State attorneys general are paving the way, as California Attorney General Rob Bonta has already subpoenaed Nvidia on how chips reached China and whether investors were misled.

According to recent reports, export controls were meant to keep America’s best chips out of China’s war machine, yet the evidence shows that Nvidia’s most sensitive chips are already fueling the Chinese military in its quest to degrade US national security. The only crime greater than smuggling these chips into the hands of the Chinese military would be our neglect in letting them get away with it.

As the line often attributed to Lenin goes, “Capitalists will sell you the rope used to hang them.”.

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • It has been revealed that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

It has been revealed that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Sources indicate that could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Recent findings suggest that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

It has been revealed that A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella states his firm’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

Industry observers note that A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the Latest York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a tech giant’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

Sources indicate that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

Sources indicate that there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “What we’ve done with our team first, we made more than a thousand millionaires,” Feldman recently mentioned on the Sourcery With Molly O’Shea channel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that employees at some of the largest tech companies are scoring major thanks to stock purchase benefits. Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman says he’s proud that his $21.7 billion AI tech giant has turned over a thousand of its staffers into millionaires. But he knows firsthand how quickly those fortunes can change—and says employees shouldn’t get too caught up in watching their net worth yo-yo.

“What we’ve done with our team first, we made more than a thousand millionaires,” Feldman recently mentioned on the Sourcery With Molly O’Shea channel. “That’s something I’m really proud of. I think that’s our job as leaders, to make our guys wealthy. We talked about the fact that we’re not in this for the short run, that the daily fluctuations are not what they should watch.”.

Recent findings suggest that as tech companies rule the U.S. stock market, all it takes is a bad earnings report or a shift in investor sentiment to send company shares on a roller-coaster ride.

Now founders and employees alike can watch their fortunes fluctuate in the span of one day. Eligible employees at Cerebras can buy firm stock directly through deductions from their paychecks at a potential 15% discount, according to the company’s 2026 employee stock purchase proposal (ESPP). In May, Cerebras had a standout IPO offering 30 million Class A shares at price of $185 per share, raising $5.55 billion.

Feldman’s share was estimated to be worth about $3.2 billion following the IPO, but the CEO warned workers against watching their wealth swing at the whim of the stock market.

In a recent development, “Change is stressful. And the vast changes in your personal wealth, both up and down, are really stressful. It’s further made challenging by the fact that your wealth is fluctuating every day—and sometimes intraday,” Feldman continued. “You try and teach people that these fluctuations that we have no control of, can’t be watched.”.

Fortune reached out to Cerebras for comment.

Feldman understands how wealth can change on a dime all too well.

As the cofounder of both Cerebras and SeaMicro with previous stints at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Force10 Networks, and Riverstone Networks, he’s seen how stock prices fluctuate in scaling tech companies.

According to recent reports, the CEO recalled that while working for a different business, the stock would swing up and down, impacting his equity. Within one day, his personal wealth changed more than his father had made in his entire lifetime, Feldman said.

In a recent development, “For a while my dad called me every day and remarked, ‘Why is your stock down?’ Like, ‘Dad, that’s not helpful. Come on, Dad. I know it’s down, but I don’t know why,’” Feldman continued during the podcast. “You have to modulate when it’s up—your psyche—and you’ve got to modulate when it’s down. And you’ve got to think about what your job is every day.”.

To help employees navigate the pressure of wealth, Feldman has some advice for workers who find themselves sitting on a chunk of tech giant stock.

While workers may hold on to their manufacturer stock to capitalize on future gains—or out of perceived loyalty to their employer—they shouldn’t be afraid to diversify, the Cerebras CEO advised.

“Most companies now, especially ones that have been around for years, have a way for, as a private manufacturer, for you to sell a little bit and pay yourself,” Feldman told Molly O’Shea. “There’s no reason for you to have 99% of your wealth in one stock. Professional investors don’t do it, and Mr. Employee, there’s no reason for you to do it either. I think it’s okay to sell a little bit.”.

He continued, “It’s not a statement on the tech giant, it’s a statement that your situation is such that it’s unwise to have 99% of your wealth or 95% of your wealth in a single company.”.

Feldman added that there’s no pressure to make moves when a worker gets a big cash gain. People may come out of the woodwork and offer financial advice for a fee, he noted, but employees can always put their wealth in a money market account and take a breather. Once they get comfortable with their situation, professionals can revisit other investment strategies. These moments of wealth also force perspective on what they want to do with their newfound coin.

Recent findings suggest that “What did I do the first time we sold the company? I paid off the house. That felt good,” Feldman explained. “I think it forces you to confront some of your values. How much you’d like to give to charity, if any? Are you the type of person that wants a super flashy car?”.

More than anything, Feldman believes that people should make their wealth work for them. With more money comes greater responsibilities—but the billionaire says it shouldn’t take the joy out of financial success.

“Once you have some cash, it’s okay to do nothing with it. And it’s designed so that you shouldn’t be more stressed. And certainly I’ve seen it have that impact on people when they got really really stressed,” Feldman noted. “It should make your life better, rather than worse.”.

It has been revealed that the last time XRP lost more than 28% in a month was February 2025, when the token fell 29.3%. That month, the crypto market was also hit by a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange on Feb. 21.

XRP did not recover right away. From March to June 2025, the token gained about 4.5% in total, according to CryptoRank. In July 2025, XRP jumped 35%, and on July 18, 2025, it set its all-time high of $3.65. On the same day, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the GENIUS Act, the country's first stablecoin law. XRP is now 73% below that record.

In a recent development, in November 2021, XRP lost 10%, and it fell another 17% in December and 25.6% in January 2022. In November 2022, the month of the FTX collapse, the token dropped 11.8%, and it lost 16.9% in December. XRP finished 2022 down about 59% and gained 20.1% in January 2023.

According to CryptoRank, XRP's median return is -10.2% in November and -4.07% in December.

SoSoValue data shows spot XRP ETFs have lost about $26 million to outflows since the start of November. About $19.1 million of that amount left the funds in the week ending Nov. 13.

On Nov. 19, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse said on CNBC that investors had been selling crypto to buy shares in substantial listings. "People are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls.

The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs, and Nvidia’s board subsequently firing him from the company he founded, is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” mentioned one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

In a recent development, although Huang’s board reinstated him on Monday in a controversial move, the roller coaster of events has pushed other CEOs to think about how their assets are connected, and potentially at risk, as a result of their personal relationships. In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

It has been revealed that “It’s totally changed the landscape,” mentioned Mazzei. “I’ve never seen this before. This was definitely substantial news in the family law space.”.

Since the Nvidia scandal broke, three clients have contacted Mazzei with requests to draft NDAs for the significant others of CEOs. They specifically cited Huang in the outreach, said Mazzei, who specializes in representing high-net-worth clients. Most of the requests are coming from the firm, not the CEO themselves, in an effort to protect the business.

“The organization is probably telling the CEO, ‘Anyone you need to date needs to sign this because we don’t want you to end up in a Jensen Huang situation,’” Mazzei mentioned.

Industry observers note that huang had at least three known affairs, two with internal Nvidia employees, and one extra controversial relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. Alice Huang is reportedly suspected by some intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy and of illegally providing Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips. The allegations are that Alice Huang is a “honeypot” who lured Jensen Huang into a relationship to get access to proprietary information.

According to recent reports, “Why honeypots work is because when you’re dating someone you’re not thinking about what they might overhear on a phone call, or see on papers lying out at home,” noted Mazzei. “They’re just in your life, overhearing a lot.”.

According to recent reports, demand for prenuptial agreements has also surged. Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. According to California law, Lori stands to come away with half of that in a potential divorce, along with shares in Nvidia.

In a recent development, it remains to be seen if Lori Huang will file for a divorce. If the couple were to decide to split up, Lori and Jensen Huang would most likely agree to a settlement prior to the divorce proceedings becoming public, notes Mazzei. Once the terms are finalized, Mazzei reckons, the couple would then go public with the news, as Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott did.

Libby Leffler, founder and CEO of thisfirst.com, an online prenup service, notes she’s seen more customers naming tech billionaires and founders as the inspiration for their agreements since the Nvidia scandal broke. Most of Leffler’s clients are founders and early employees at pre-IPO companies, especially in California and Newly introduced York. Every time a public figure’s divorce or prenup makes headlines, Leffler’s inbound requests jump, but the naming of tech CEOs this time is different.

Industry observers note that “People used to name-check celebs, but now they are name-checking tech CEOs,” Leffler tells Fortune. “What they really mean is that they want to feel as protected as they assume those people are.” The most referenced arrangement is Jeff Bezos’s rumored prenuptial agreement with Lauren Sánchez, who became his second wife in 2025.

“Your relationship and your cap table are more connected than people think, and founders are seeing that play out,” Leffler said.

Recent findings suggest that mazzei also noted a surge in prenup requests, specifically coming from Anthropic employees. When the organization went public at a $1.5 trillion valuation on Nov. 19—a week after Huang’s ousting—it minted thousands of multimillionaires among the company’s relatively small staff of 5,300. The average fortune of its non-founding staff is roughly $44 million, although nearly 600 pocketed at least $100 million.

According to recent reports, mazzei could not link the Anthropic employees’ requests to Nvidia directly, although the Huangs’ lack of a prenup may have spooked them. In general, many of them are on the younger side, and Mazzei noted that among younger generations prenups are becoming more common.

Stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 include a full closure and a Black Friday early close, plus Christmas dates, regular Nasdaq hours and extended sessions.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving week 2026 squeezes the U.S. stock trading calendar into a shorter stretch than usual. Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists the market as closed on Thursday, November 26. It then highlights an early close at 1:00 p.m. on Friday, November 27, the day widely known as Black Friday. Anyone checking stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 needs both dates in view.

In a recent development, A normal session on the Nasdaq Stock Market runs Monday through Friday, from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. A full closure removes that session entirely. An early close trims the day, and the schedule lists 1:00 p.m. as the cutoff on the affected dates.

Recent findings suggest that those changes matter for anyone who places orders, sets price alerts or prepares trades around the closing bell. An order meant for the last hour of a normal day may need different timing on a shortened one. Alerts and standing instructions tied to a 4:00 p.m. finish may need adjusting too.

December brings a second set of changes. Nasdaq's schedule lists another 1:00 p.m. early close on Thursday, December 24, followed by a full closure on Friday, December 25. Christmas Day is the final entry in Nasdaq's 2026 table. Earlier in the year, the same schedule lists Labor Day, September 7, 2026, as a closure. It is the last holiday on that list before Thanksgiving.

Holiday dates are only part of the picture. Nasdaq also publishes hours for pre-market and after-hours sessions, and some of its options venues trade until 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time. Extended-hours trading comes with thinner participation and bigger price swings, and access varies by broker.

This guide covers a selection of dates and hours from Nasdaq's published schedule, not every entry in it. The slides that follow explain the Thanksgiving closure, the shortened Black Friday session, the Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes, the regular trading day and the extended sessions. Nasdaq offers downloadable trading calendars for 2026 and 2027, along with links to its Nordic and Nasdaq Canada schedules.

It has been revealed that the U.S. stock market is closed all day on Thursday, November 26, 2026, for Thanksgiving. Nasdaq $NDAQ lists the date as a full closure on its 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule. No regular trading session runs that day.

A full closure is different from a shortened day. No session is scheduled to open, and none is scheduled to close. The date drops out of the trading calendar entirely.

Timing matters for anyone who planned to act on Thursday. An order intended for the holiday has to be placed during an earlier session or held until trading resumes. Investors who rebalance on a fixed schedule or track a position into the close can account for the missing day ahead of time.

The holiday extends beyond stock exchanges. The Federal Reserve System includes Thanksgiving Day on its list of observed holidays.

Sources indicate that on Nasdaq's 2026 calendar, the closure listed immediately before Thanksgiving is Labor Day, Monday, September 7, 2026. No other holiday sits between those two dates on the schedule.

Investors who want the dates saved can download Nasdaq's 2026 trading calendar from the same schedule page. The 2026 schedule on that page covers U.S. markets. Nasdaq links separately to holiday schedules for its Nordic markets and for Nasdaq Canada.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists Friday, November 27, 2026, as an early close, with trading ending at 1:00 p.m. The market opens that day, but the session is shorter than a normal one.

That Friday follows Thanksgiving Day, Thursday, November 26, 2026, when the market stays closed. Investors returning from the holiday get one abbreviated session before the weekend.

In a recent development, the early close changes the trading window, not the trading date. November 27 still counts as a market day. Anyone who usually acts late in the session has less time to do it.

The schedule's entry for November 27 gives the 1:00 p.m. time without naming a time zone. Readers should confirm with their broker which time zone applies and what the local equivalent is, rather than assume it.

Anyone planning to place, change or cancel orders that Friday should ask their broker how it handles the shortened day. That check can cover whether pre-market or after-hours trading is offered on November 27. It can also cover when Nasdaq's options venues stop trading that day.

Industry observers note that the stock market closes early at 1:00 p.m. on Thursday, December 24, 2026, and stays shut all day on Friday, December 25, 2026, for Christmas Day. Both dates appear on Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule.

It has been revealed that christmas Eve brings a shortened session rather than a day off. Trading opens as usual, then stops at the 1:00 p.m. cutoff listed for that date. The cutoff removes the late afternoon that a normal weekday session would include.

In a recent development, the schedule leaves some questions about December 24 open. It does not say whether pre-market and after-hours sessions run that day. It also does not give closing times for Nasdaq's options venues on early-close dates. Anyone planning trades in those sessions should check how their broker handles the day.

In a recent development, christmas Day is a full closure, with no regular trading session at all. In 2026, December 26 and 27 fall on a Saturday and a Sunday. The Nasdaq Stock Market's regular hours run Monday through Friday only. That leaves three consecutive days without a regular session, from Friday through Sunday. Monday, December 28, does not appear on the holiday table.

In a recent development, christmas Day also matters for some investment funds whose business days follow the market calendar. One fund's supplement describes its business days as those when both the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York are open. The same filing lists Christmas Day among the holidays when the fund is closed. The filing also treats weekends as non-operating days for both institutions.

Industry observers note that christmas Day is the last entry in Nasdaq's 2026 holiday table. Investors planning further ahead can download a 2027 trading calendar from the same page.

It has been revealed that the Nasdaq $NDAQ Stock Market trades Monday through Friday from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Six Nasdaq options venues keep trading until 4:15 p.m. ET, later than the stock market's closing bell.

In a recent development, that regular stock session lasts six and a half hours each weekday. It is the baseline for every date on Nasdaq's 2026 holiday schedule. The Thanksgiving, Black Friday, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes all alter this window.

It has been revealed that the six options venues with the later close are Nasdaq PHLX, The Nasdaq Options Market (NOM), Nasdaq ISE, Nasdaq GEMX, Nasdaq Texas Options and Nasdaq MRX. Each one trades from 9:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. ET on a regular day. Options trading on these markets continues for a quarter of an hour after the main stock session ends.

Two other Nasdaq equities venues follow the same clock as the main market. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) equities and Nasdaq PSX both trade from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET. Their sessions open and close alongside the Nasdaq Stock Market, without the extra time the options venues get.

In a recent development, trading hours are not the same as system hours. Nasdaq lists a separate system window for each venue. Those windows are wider than the regular trading session, and they differ from one venue to the next.

Industry observers note that the Nasdaq Stock Market system runs from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET, a span of 16 hours. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) runs from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ET, a 12-hour window. Nasdaq PSX runs from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET, or nine hours. Nasdaq PHLX and the options markets run from 7:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. ET, a span of nine hours and 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, every one of those system windows opens before 9:30 a.m. ET and closes after 4:00 p.m. ET. Investors who need to know exactly when an order can execute on a given venue, including during shortened holiday sessions, can confirm the details with their broker.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's pre-market session runs from 4:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. ET, and its after-hours session runs from 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. Both windows fall outside the regular weekday session.

The sessions connect directly to the regular day. Pre-market trading ends at 9:30 a.m. ET, the moment the regular session opens. After-hours trading begins at 4:00 p.m. ET, the moment it closes.

In a recent development, together, the two windows add nine and a half hours to a normal weekday. The pre-market stretch lasts five and a half hours. The after-hours stretch lasts four. The regular session between them runs six and a half hours.

Recent findings suggest that those times describe Nasdaq's own sessions, not what every investor can reach. Nasdaq notes that some brokers set different hours for extended trading. It also notes that not every online broker offers extended-hours trading at all. Anyone who wants to place orders before the opening bell or after the close should confirm both points with their brokerage first.

Trading conditions also differ outside regular hours. Nasdaq warns that extended sessions carry lower liquidity, which means fewer participants are buying and selling. It also warns of higher volatility, with prices liable to swing more widely than during the regular day.

Holiday weeks add another variable. Nasdaq's 2026 schedule lists Thanksgiving Day, November 26, and Christmas Day, December 25, as full closures, with no regular session on either date. It lists Friday, November 27, and Thursday, December 24, as early closes at 1:00 p.m.

It has been revealed that the schedule does not say whether pre-market or after-hours trading takes place on those two shortened days, or at what times. Investors who plan to trade outside regular hours on November 27 or December 24 should ask their broker how those sessions will be handled.

  • With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue indicates that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.

This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.

With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue indicates that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.

Previous ETF data shows that March remains the only month in which spot XRP ETFs have recorded net outflows since their launch.

While it still stands as the record outflow month for XRP ETFs, investors withdrew about $31.16 million from the funds during that month.

This means that the persistent withdrawals seen this month have brought the November outflow dangerously close to its previous monthly record seen in March.

Apparently, the spot XRP ETFs are on track to close November as their worst-performing month since launch, with just about $1 million left to hit the record.

Further data also shows that the spot XRP ETFs have yet to record a single day of net inflows throughout November, as the persistent price decline has caused investors to slow down their purchases.

As such, the influx of fresh capital into the spot XRP ETF market has remained on hold amid growing market uncertainty and a shift in investor sentiment.

#87535. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1316 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The latest funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of substantial names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

It has been revealed that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis stated in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Recent findings suggest that marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

According to recent reports, lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight firm acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a upcoming startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

According to recent reports, since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The organization isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Sources indicate that its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders remarked. A second, larger site using AMD’s fresh Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company claims it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

It has been revealed that srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe states gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

It has been revealed that coreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

In a recent development, marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The organization’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

It has been revealed that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis noted. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

It has been revealed that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Industry observers note that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Sources indicate that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one significant customer that could pull out.

Industry observers note that ultimately, Lewis noted he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

According to recent reports, updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

#87534. Latest Update: Private equity deals in sports doubled in the past two years: Investors see it as an ‘institutional-grade asset class,’ Apollo’s Torsten Slok indicates

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (829 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Private equity deals in sports doubled in the past two years: Investors see it as an ‘institutional-grade asset class,’ Apollo’s Torsten Slok indicates

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Private equity is coming for America’s favorite pastime, America’s game, and almost every other sport.
  • “Private equity deals in global sports have roughly doubled from about 100 a year in 2021–2023 to almost 200 in both 2024 and 2025, a sign that investors increasingly see sports as an institutional-grade asset class,” Slok wrote in a Nov.
  • The investment boom isn’t just limited to stakes in pro teams, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Private equity is coming for America’s favorite pastime, America’s game, and almost every other sport. Private equity firms are buying into sports at twice the pace they were a few years ago, according to Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok.

“Private equity deals in global sports have roughly doubled from about 100 a year in 2021–2023 to almost 200 in both 2024 and 2025, a sign that investors increasingly see sports as an institutional-grade asset class,” Slok wrote in a Nov. 22 analysis.

The investment boom isn’t just limited to stakes in pro teams, however. Private equity firms also target the businesses that supply, support and monetize sports, from equipment manufacturers to talent agencies to training facilities.

On Nov. 19, Swiss investment firm Partners Group agreed to acquire a majority stake in Rawlings Sporting Goods—the manufacturer of baseballs, gloves, bats, and protective equipment for MLB. The company serves as the league’s official supplier of game balls, gloves, helmets, face guards, and bases. The league itself owned a stake in the company as well, meaning unlike the minority stakes leagues allow in their teams, the deal gives a private equity firm control.

According to Partners Group, MLB and Rawlings’ existing shareholders will retain meaningful ownership while also giving the Swiss firm exposure to Rawlings’ broader business—which includes brands like Easton and Combat, as well as D-BAT Academies, a network of 228 indoor baseball and softball training facilities.

According to recent reports, “Rawlings’ iconic brands and training footprint helps reinforce participation in America’s pastime and has credibility with consumers and athletes across all ages,” Partners Group managing director, private equity goods and products, Thomas Clark said in a press release. “We look forward to working with [CEO Ron Ostrowski], the Rawlings team, and MLB as long-term partners.”.

Apollo has its own sports arm as well: In August, Apollo Sports Capital became a “strategic investment partner” to MLB’s most iconic franchise—the New York Yankees. The deal was a $2.6 billion financing agreement with Yankee Global Enterprises, the team’s holding organization, supporting the “continued growth” of the Yankees franchise while also refinancing its existing debt.

According to recent reports, “Teams and leagues might embrace capital for any number of reasons: to support operating costs, update aging facilities or develop new venues, invest in new technologies, or grow their global reach,” Deloitte’s 2026 Global Sports Industry Outlook report read. “But outside investment brings greater scrutiny, new challenges, and rising expectations around transparency, governance, and financial rigor.”.

Industry observers note that for decades, professional sports restricted private equity firms and other institutional investors from owning stakes in their teams. Instead, franchises were controlled by wealthy individuals, families, or ownership groups—mainly from the leagues’ concern about preserving control over teams and maintaining structure.

Sources indicate that that began changing in 2019, however, when Major League Baseball became the first major U.S. professional sports league to permit private equity investments in franchises. The NBA and Major League Soccer followed in 2020, and the NHL lifted restrictions in 2021. The NFL became the last of the four major American sports leagues to approve private equity ownership, in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that but those permissions came with limits. According to Sportico, MLB allowed institutional investors to own up to 30% of a franchise, with a single fund capped at 15%. The NBA and NHL permit up to 30% institutional ownership per team as well, but cap individual funds at 20%. The NFL has the strictest ownership rules, only allowing approved private equity firms to own a combined stake of up to 10% in a team—and only 10% in an individual fund as well.

And the owners have taken advantage of that influx of capital. Outside money helps owners pay for stadium construction, arena renovations, player contracts, and the development of surrounding entertainment districts, all without having to foot the full bill themselves.

For example, the Buffalo Bills created an arrangement in 2024 following the NFL’s lifted restrictions to sell 21% of the team’s stake to a group of limited partners—which included a 10% investment from private equity firm Arctos Partners. The transaction came as the Bills were building their fresh stadium, when projected costs rose from $1.4 billion to $2.1 billion.

But the benefit for private equity owners exists as well. Professional sports teams have access to multiple revenue streams, including broadcasting rights, ticket sales, sponsorships, merchandise, licensing, and stadium-related businesses. The five major U.S. professional sports leagues generated approximately $60 billion in combined revenue in 2025, according to Congress. The estimated combined value of their franchises reached approximately $560 billion that year.

“The new model of baseball—or basketball, football—is teams becoming media companies and transcending a local marketplace,” Rashaun Williams, founder and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners, which held a minority stake in the newly relocated Las Vegas Athletics MLB team, previously told Fortune. “They’re finding ways to diversify their revenue and monetize that fan base 365 days a year.”.

Dogecoin co-founder Billy Markus, known on X as Shibetoshi Nakamoto, reacted to the recent market decline, which saw over $2.56 billion in liquidations. He hinted at weak demand as a possible reason behind the massive sell-off.

Markus earlier wrote in a post that "Black Friday came early." This came as the broader financial markets dropped, not just crypto: tech stocks, gold, copper, and Asian equities all fell.

Recent findings suggest that markus’s post garnered attention from the Dogecoin community and the wider crypto community. A Dogecoin community member responded: “Am I retarded for thinking crypto is about to go up?”.

@alphadoge777 well it always goes up and down 🤣 but the market has been looking pretty low demand for awhile now.

"Well, it always goes up and down," Markus mentioned, pointing to crypto's inherent volatility and adding that the market had been experiencing "pretty low demand for a while now.".

His comments come as the crypto market continues to crash, highlighting concerns about the lack of buying interest needed to prop up prices.

Markus did not point to a specific catalyst for the decline, but his remarks highlight an important ingredient for a bullish comeback in the market: demand.

According to recent reports, the crypto market selloff deepened on Saturday, with Bitcoin hitting its lowest level since September 2024 and extending a brutal run for risk assets. Dogecoin was trading in the red, down 8.13% in the last 24 hours to $0.528 and down 16% weekly. Dogecoin fell to $0.05 earlier on Saturday, a low not seen since June 2022.

Data from Coinglass at press time show that $2.56 billion was liquidated in crypto positions over the past 24 hours; longs accounted for 89.2% of this total, at $2.28 billion, while short liquidations came in at $276,040.

Analysts pointed to rising real, or inflation-adjusted, U.S. Treasury yields as a key driver of the ongoing sell-off, which extends a bear market that began in October of last year.

Crypto investors are searching for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. The broader crypto market has dropped since the Clarity Act faced a setback in September.

#87532. 8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2965 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight of the largest MLB deals for Japanese players, from Ohtani's $700 million to Murakami's $34 million, and what each total leaves out.
  • In a recent development, major league teams now compete to sign the best players from Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league, and fans tend to judge each of those signings by the total written on the contract.
  • Deadlines also shape the price, and they favor the team most willing to spend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight of the largest MLB deals for Japanese players, from Ohtani's $700 million to Murakami's $34 million, and what each total leaves out.

In a recent development, major league teams now compete to sign the best players from Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league, and fans tend to judge each of those signings by the total written on the contract. That total leaves out a second payment, because a team that signs a posted Japanese star pays the player and also pays the Japanese club that let him go. MLB.com reports that the Yankees paid Masahiro Tanaka's Japanese club a posting fee separate from his contract. The Blue Jays owed the same kind of fee to Kazuma Okamoto's club under MLB's agreement with NPB, with that money kept outside his contract, according to CBC. The second bill is a standing part of the price of Japanese talent. It keeps rising on deals past $50 million, with the Japanese club taking 15% of any value above that mark, according to CBS Sports. None of that money appears in the headline figure, so the total fans quote covers only part of what a team spends.

Deadlines also shape the price, and they favor the team most willing to spend. Once his club posts him, a Japanese player has 45 days to negotiate with MLB teams, according to MLB.com. Every interested team has to make its best offer within the same few weeks. The final number reflects how many teams wanted the player and how badly they needed him, as much as his record in Japan. The years and dollars on paper can also differ from what a team actually pays and how long the player stays. Money deferred for years costs a team less than money paid now, and an opt-out can end a deal well before its last season. Fans who compare totals learn less than it seems about who is the better player, and the smallest deal can turn out to be the best one.

ESPN set out to rank the largest MLB deals that Japanese players have signed, including the Yankees' 2014 contract for Masahiro Tanaka, the Cubs' deal for Teruaki Sato and the White Sox's deal for Munetaka Murakami. Each of those totals is the money a team promised, and it is best read as a starting point. Behind a total can sit a fee owed to a club in Japan, pay that arrives years later, an exit the player controls or a team in a hurry to fill a hole. Read that way, the order of these deals states more about what each team promised than about what each player turned out to be worth.

Shohei Ohtani signed the richest contract a Japanese player has ever received, and the Dodgers paid it for a star they had already watched in the majors. Los Angeles committed $700 million over 10 years to a player who had spent six seasons across town with the Angels, according to ESPN. Nobody had to guess whether his game would carry over from Japan, so the hard question about the deal is how the Dodgers built it. The Associated Press reports that 97% of the money was deferred without interest when he signed in 2023. Almost all of the record total is a promise to pay later, and the question that matters is when the Dodgers actually hand the money over.

According to recent reports, the Dodgers will pay most of Ohtani's money long after he signed, and they will spread it across a decade. The deferred payments arrive each July 1 from 2034 through 2043, according to The Associated Press. A dollar paid that far in the future, with no interest added, is worth less than a dollar paid today, and the Dodgers' real cost is below $700 million. Nobody needs to settle on an exact figure for that gap to matter. Ohtani's total can't be compared directly with a contract that pays a player during the seasons he plays.

The 10 years are also less certain than they look, because Ohtani can leave for reasons that have nothing to do with how he plays. The Associated Press reports that the 2023 contract lets him opt out if Mark Walter stops being the controlling owner or if Andrew Friedman leaves as president of baseball operations. A change in the front office, rather than a slump, could end the decade early.

The record contract puts off most of its payments for a decade and leaves its length in the hands of the team's owner and its top baseball executive.

The Dodgers committed more money to Yoshinobu Yamamoto than any team had committed to a player moving straight from Japan to the majors, and they did it before he had thrown a major league pitch. His $325 million contract is the largest for a player arriving directly from Japan, according to ESPN. The Los Angeles Times reports that he was 25 when he signed in 2023, and that before bidding opened, he was expected to command at least $200 million. Clubs judged him on his pitching in Japan, where he won the Pacific League's MVP award in three consecutive seasons. Teams kept raising their offers well past that early estimate, and his final price measures how hard clubs competed for him as much as how good he was.

The Dodgers bid the highest because signing Yamamoto served a plan built around Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani helped recruit him, taking part with teammates Betts and Freeman in the meeting the Dodgers held with Yamamoto at their ballpark, according to the Los Angeles Times. "It was important to Shohei that this wasn't the one move we were gonna make, and I think anyone who has watched us operate over the years, we're trying to add really good players at every turn," Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers' president of baseball operations, told the Los Angeles Times in 2023. A team that had made that promise to its biggest star had little reason to stop bidding at the early estimate. When several teams compete for one player, the team with the most pressing plan usually decides the final price.

In a recent development, so far, Yamamoto has pitched well enough to justify the Dodgers' spending. He earned the World Series MVP award in 2025, according to MLB.com. Paying well above the early estimate looks less like a mistake when the player is judged the most valuable performer in the World Series. The competition among teams raised what the Dodgers spent, but it did not make the deal a bad one.

The Dodgers paid extra to sign him, and so far he has pitched like the player they were bidding for.

Industry observers note that the Yankees offered Masahiro Tanaka a sum that few pitchers of any background had received. Newly introduced York signed him for $155 million over seven years in 2014, according to ESPN. MLB.com reports that it was then the fifth-highest contract ever given to a pitcher, and only Kershaw, Verlander, Hernandez and Sabathia had been paid more. The Yankees put a pitcher who came directly from Nippon Professional Baseball, and who had never thrown a major league inning, in the same pay bracket as those four.

According to recent reports, new York spent more to get Tanaka than the figure that ranks him. The Yankees also paid Rakuten, the Japanese club that posted him, $20 million for the right to sign him, according to MLB.com. That payment bought permission alone, and none of it went to Tanaka. The Yankees' real bet on him was larger than his ranked total.

Industry observers note that the Yankees made their case for Tanaka entirely on what he had done in Japan. In 2013, his last season with Rakuten, he went 24-0 with a 1.27 ERA, according to MLB.com. No team had seen him face major league hitters, so that season highlighted promise rather than proof. The Yankees still bid as if they would never get another chance. "That was our one shot, and we took it very seriously," Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said in 2014.

The Yankees paid to find out what Tanaka could do against major league hitters, not to buy a record he had already set there.

The Chicago Cubs paid one of the highest prices ever for a hitter coming from Japan, and they paid it for the best batting season any player there had put together in years. ESPN reports that Sato agreed to $120 million over six years with the Cubs, the third-largest deal for a player from Japan's league. Sato became the first Triple Crown winner in Japan since Munetaka Murakami's 2022 season, according to CBS Sports. The Cubs are paying for the one skill Sato showed best, his power. They are not paying for a hitter without flaws.

Sato misses the ball far more often than a typical major league hitter, and the Cubs signed him anyway. He made contact on 66% of his swings, against a major league average of 77%, according to CBS Sports. That gap means he will likely strike out more than most hitters once he faces major league pitching. Chicago is betting that his home runs will outweigh the empty swings, and the six-year term shows the team expects that power to last for years. "Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll," CBS Sports writer Dayn Perry wrote.

The Cubs took that risk because the departure of two regulars left them short of a bat. Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki both left in free agency, according to CBS Sports, and together they were worth 7.8 wins above a replacement player in 2026. Sato is being asked to replace a large share of that production by himself. Chicago looks to use him in left or right field, even though he is known mainly as a first or third baseman, and his biggest adjustment will be the better pitching he faces. Sato's price reflects how badly Chicago needed a bat as much as it reflects the quality of his bat.

In a recent development, toronto turned to Kaima Taira after several other starting pitchers it pursued signed elsewhere. The Blue Jays agreed to pay him $80 million over five years, with a $5 million bonus and an opt-out, according to ESPN. Tarik Skubal chose the Latest York Mets even though Toronto had reportedly offered him nine years and $420 million, according to USA TODAY. Two more starters the team went after also landed with other clubs, with Trevor Rogers joining the Chicago Cubs and Freddy Peralta joining the Baltimore Orioles. MLB's labor deal expires Dec. 1, and Toronto chose to fill its rotation before that deadline rather than keep searching. The team paid Taira's price out of need and failed pursuits as much as for anything he did on the mound.

Industry observers note that toronto is paying mostly for Taira's return to starting. After working strictly in relief as a closer in 2025, he moved back into a rotation in 2026 and led every qualified starter in Japan with a 1.36 ERA, according to USA TODAY. He has never thrown more than 150 innings in a season, yet Toronto will likely slot him third in its rotation in 2027. The Blue Jays are betting less on the ERA than on whether his arm can last through a full season of starts.

Sources indicate that the opt-out puts much of the reward in Taira's hands. If he holds up as a starter, he can leave and look for a better deal before the five years run out. If his arm wears down, the choice to stay is his as well, and Toronto keeps the cost.

Need brought Taira to Toronto, and his own success could take him away.

Industry observers note that toronto paid Kazuma Okamoto a solid price rather than a superstar's price. The Blue Jays gave him a four-year, $60 million contract, which tops the $54 million deal Tatsuya Imai signed, according to ESPN. Bringing him to Toronto cost the team more than his contract. Toronto must also send $10,875,000 to the Yomiuri Giants, the club he played for in Japan, according to CBC. A contender spent that much on a hitter who isn't a headline star because it needed a third baseman.

Toronto finished last season without a regular third baseman. Addison Barger and Ernie Clement split the starts at the position almost evenly, CBC reports, and neither player held the job. With this contract, the team bought a full-time answer at a position it had been filling day to day.

Sources indicate that the Blue Jays are betting that Okamoto's power will carry over to the majors. He arrives directly from Japan's league with 248 career home runs, according to CBC, and he hit every one of them in Japan. Toronto paid for a proven record that major league pitching has yet to test. It did not pay for star power.

According to recent reports, okamoto settles one position in an infield that is otherwise uncertain. Bo Bichette is a free agent who has not re-signed, CBC reports, so Toronto may still have a hole elsewhere in the infield. The team put its largest money that winter into pitching. In the same winter it committed $60 million to Okamoto, Toronto gave Dylan Cease a seven-year, $210 million deal. That made Okamoto a supporting piece for a team spending heavily to win now.

Toronto paid Okamoto's price as a team in a hurry to fill a gap, and the figure is no measure of how good he will turn out to be.

Sources indicate that tatsuya Imai earned a place among the largest MLB contracts signed by Japanese players, though near the low end of that group, when the Astros gave him three years and $54 million, according to ESPN. Those three years look like a firm commitment from Houston. But Imai can opt out after the 2026 season, MLB.com reports, and he can opt out again after 2027, which means he could become a free agent after one or two seasons. The $54 million reveals what the Astros promised him. How long he stays is Imai's decision.

In a recent development, imai could take a short deal because his results have held up for years. He has posted a 2.18 ERA since 2023, according to MLB.com. That mark covers several seasons of work, so his success does not rest on a single strong year. His camp put him on the same level as Yoshinobu Yamamoto. "Certainly, he's done everything that Yamamoto's done in NPB," Scott Boras, Imai's agent, said. Even with that standing, Imai signed for three years instead of locking in his prime at a fixed rate. He kept the right to ask for a new price soon. The short term reads as Imai's wager on himself rather than a sign that teams doubted him.

In a recent development, the Astros accepted a deal that could end early because they needed starting pitchers right away. Three Astros pitchers had Tommy John surgery in 2025, according to MLB.com. Pitchers usually miss more than a season after that operation, so the Astros faced the coming year with holes in their rotation. They also expect to lose Framber Valdez, a mainstay of that rotation, in free agency. A team that short of starters now gains more from one or two excellent seasons than from waiting for a longer commitment.

The Astros are guaranteed to pay Imai $54 million, but they carry the risk that his success will take him to another team before the three years are up.

Industry observers note that the White Sox may have paid too little for Munetaka Murakami rather than too much. Chicago signed him to a two-year, $34 million contract, according to ESPN, the smallest of the biggest deals Japanese players have signed with MLB teams. For that price, the team got power that only one other Japanese-born hitter has shown in the majors. Murakami and Shohei Ohtani are the only Japanese-born players with 35 or more home runs in a season, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Murakami's contract is the smallest in this group, but his power puts him in the same manufacturer as the most celebrated Japanese hitter in the game.

Industry observers note that chicago has already received a full slugger's season from the first year of a short deal. By Sept. 25 of his rookie season, Murakami had hit 35 home runs, the Chicago Sun-Times reports, and only Jose Abreu and Ron Kittle had reached that mark as White Sox rookies. Murakami does most of his damage by pulling the ball toward right field, but 29% of his home runs have gone to center field or the left side. His power reaches more than one part of the park. One season of that production already makes a $34 million price look low.

Murakami came to Chicago straight from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball, and one season later he is an key hitter for a White Sox team chasing the Cleveland Guardians in the AL Central. His value is being tested in games that matter now, and the bargain depends on him staying at this level. "We know how impactful he can be when he's right and feeling good," White Sox manager Will Venable said, as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. Chicago signed Murakami for only two seasons, and half of that time is nearly over. One poor season could erase the bargain.

Chicago got a historic return in the first year of the smallest of these deals, and only Murakami's second season can show whether he can repeat it.
