  • Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.
  • This wasn’t your original career path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

This wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he said, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very promptly, sold after about four or five years.

In a recent development, what inspired STRONG?My housemate showed me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

According to recent reports, most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

Recent findings suggest that now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

Was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The major one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. They were terrified to jump on a reformer. So the TVs, although they’re not liked by the traditionalists, gave us a huge uptake, particularly with male consumers. It was huge for us.

Your Instagram handle is just “Strong.” How on earth did you get that?Do you remember when domain names were getting really expensive? Like imagine strong.com. It’s probably worth half a million dollars. I had some friends that were trying to open businesses and trying to get these domain names, and I thought, “Well, I’m gonna start acquiring one-word Instagram names,” because Instagram was really taking off at the time. And so I had Strong, I had Cultivate, I had Ram. So I just held onto them. And then when I went to Orange County and I did the workout, I thought, “How does this workout make me feel? Not only do I need to be physically strong, but I need to be mentally strong to get through this.” And so it just made sense to call it STRONG Pilates, and now we’re here. At one point, it was getting tagged every 30 seconds all around the world, and I would just sit there watching it.

#87530. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (784 w)
📖 Baca

On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years.
  • Industry observers note that most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first.
  • Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Industry observers note that most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services unveiled on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

Industry observers note that by recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”.

According to recent reports, seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

In a recent development, by then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Industry observers note that against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

Recent findings suggest that with fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” noted Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”.

That job falls to the fresh Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t initiative on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

It has been revealed that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith remarked the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he stated.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which states it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

Recent findings suggest that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he mentioned. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a recent development, his one example was an unnamed manufacturer that wants to build in Finland. Google revealed a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a substantial technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the organization for a briefing.

In a recent development, smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and stated Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

In a recent development, he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the organization “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Sources indicate that outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

According to recent reports, smith remarked the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

Sources indicate that ten college football coaches carry buyouts between $49.5 million and $105.1 million. See what each price states about the school.

Ohio State has made one of the largest promises any school has made to keep its coach. The school would owe Ryan Day $70.9 million if it fired him, the second-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated, and his salary ranks among the top 10 in the sport. Ohio State made that commitment to a coach who had already delivered. Day won the national title in 2024, according to CBS Sports. With a promise that large, Ohio State was declaring that Day was the coach it meant to keep, more than it was buying him insurance.

Industry observers note that A disappointing season has turned that promise into a cost Ohio State has to weigh. The Buckeyes lost four games in 2026, according to CBS Sports, a heavy total for a team that had won it all two seasons earlier. The cost of acting has also fallen since the $70.9 million figure was dated Dec. 1, 2025. A firing once the 2026 season ends would leave Ohio State with a $57.5 million bill, a figure dated Nov. 21, 2026. The drop comes from how the contract is built. Day's buyout is set as a fixed sum for each remaining year rather than a share of his remaining salary, so the total shrinks as each season passes. The longer the school waits, the less it would pay to make a change, and the less protection Day gets from his contract.

Texas would face such a large bill to change coaches because the school made its biggest promise to Sarkisian only recently. Firing him would cost Texas $60.3 million, the fourth-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated. Longhorns Wire reports that Texas signed the deal in 2025 and committed to Sarkisian through 2031. Nearly all of that long promise has yet to be paid. The size of the figure reveals how strongly Texas bet on its coach a short time ago, more than how secure his job is today.

According to recent reports, texas is facing a test of that bet much sooner than the school planned when it signed the deal. The team held the No. 1 ranking only two weeks earlier, according to Longhorns Wire, and the fall since then has been fast enough that people now discuss a firing openly. "I believe, personally, that after Texas loses its third game (Texas athletic director) Chris Del Conte has an honest conversation about the firing of Steve Sarkisian," Cole Thompson, co-host of the SEC Unfiltered Podcast, told Longhorns Wire. Texas already has a possible interim coach on staff in defensive coordinator Will Muschamp. With a replacement in the building, the size of the $60.3 million check is the main reason for Texas to hold back.

Mike Norvell's contract promised him far more protection than his paycheck would suggest. Florida State agreed to a $58.7 million buyout, the sixth-largest among football coaches, even though his salary ranked only 45th in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. The school wrote the deal to make firing him very costly, not to pay him like one of the game's top earners. A price that large is meant to make a school think hard before it acts. Florida State fired Norvell on the Sunday after a loss to Clemson, The Post and Courier reports, and the size of the bill did nothing to slow the decision. The $58.7 million figure is dated Dec. 1, 2025, and is not a confirmed payout, so what Florida State will end up paying is still unsettled.

At Indiana, the cost of firing Curt Cignetti moved well ahead of what the school was paying him. Indiana agreed to a buyout of $56.7 million, the eighth-largest among college football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated, even though his salary ranked only 18th in the sport. The school promised far more to keep him than it paid him to coach. Indiana used the buyout to show how badly it wanted to hold on to Cignetti, and it made that commitment before his paycheck matched it.

The gap opened because Cignetti won so quickly that other schools had good reason to want him. The $56.7 million figure dates to Dec. 1, 2025, before his biggest season was over. Indiana went on to finish 16-0 with a national title win over Miami, according to The Gazette. Each of those wins made him more costly to lose, and Indiana gave him a raise after the buyout figure was fixed.

Illinois has made Bret Bielema one of the most expensive coaches in college football to fire, and the cost runs well ahead of where his pay ranks. His $49.5 million buyout is the 10th-largest among football coaches, while his salary ranks 19th in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. The cost is high because Illinois has committed to him for a long time, not because it pays him like a star. The News-Gazette reports that Illinois has extended Bielema's contract for a second time and that the deal now runs six years. The price of firing him reflects the school's own decision to renew its bet on Bielema more than any judgment of what other schools would pay him.

Recent findings suggest that at the top of college football, firing a head coach has become one of the most expensive decisions a university can make. Schools have shown they will pay sums in the tens of millions of dollars to change direction. The Associated Press reports that Texas A&M owed Jimbo Fisher more than $75 million when it decided to start over. LSU also accepted a large buyout to part ways with Brian Kelly, according to CBS Sports. Both schools chose to pay that price rather than keep a coach they no longer wanted. A buyout's size alone doesn't decide whether a coach keeps his job. It sets the price a school must accept to make a change, and the wealthiest programs in the sport have shown they will accept it.

In a recent development, the figure attached to a coach is less settled than it looks, because it marks the most a school might owe rather than what the school ends up paying. The Associated Press reports that the amount depends largely on how many years remain on a contract. A school that waits a season before acting owes less than one that acts today. A school can also bargain. Penn State owed James Franklin $49 million when it let him go, CBS Sports reports, and the two sides settled on $9 million. That changes how to read any coach's price tag. Each figure describes a contract on one date. It says as much about what a school was willing to promise as about how secure the coach really is.

Sports Illustrated set out to identify which college football coaches would cost the most to fire, at programs ranging from Indiana and Illinois to Georgia and Florida State. Each figure is the price a school would pay to change course, not a measure of a coach's salary or skill. Some of these contracts were written to keep a winning coach in place. For those schools, a large number is a statement of how much they want to keep the man they have. Other contracts are being tested by losing seasons, and for those schools the figure is the real cost of a change they may be weighing. At least one school on the list has already made that change anyway.

According to recent reports, georgia has made the largest commitment to its coach of any school in college football. As of Dec. 1, 2025, firing Kirby Smart would have cost the school $105.1 million, far more than any other known buyout in the sport, according to Sports Illustrated. Georgia faces a bill that large because of a promise it made, not because of a penalty clause. Bleacher Report reports that the school fully guaranteed Smart's deal if it fires him without cause through Dec. 31, 2028, and that the guarantee drops to 85% after that. Georgia's full promise therefore covers the next few seasons, and for those seasons the school has chosen to face the sport's highest price if it ever wants a change.

According to recent reports, the contract binds Georgia far more than it binds Smart. Smart could walk away for a small part of what Georgia would owe to push him out, paying $5 million through the end of 2026, according to Bleacher Report. Smart, not the school, holds the easy way out. If another job ever tempts him, the decision is his.

According to recent reports, georgia has little reason to want a change, because Smart keeps winning. Under Smart, Georgia claimed back-to-back national titles in the 2021 and 2022 seasons and holds a 46-3 record over that stretch, according to Bleacher Report. That kind of winning makes the guarantee easy for the school to stand behind. Georgia wrote the largest buyout in college football to protect a coach who almost never loses. At a school with a struggling coach, a buyout is a price to weigh. At Georgia, it is mostly a statement of intent.

Georgia has promised more than any other school to keep its coach, and Smart is the one who decides whether the deal holds.

A smaller bill alone may not settle Day's future. A school should fire a coach only when it has a clearly better replacement in mind, and the market for coaches is thin right now. Day has gone 89-16 at Ohio State, according to CBS Sports, and has won the large majority of his games. For a change to pay off, Ohio State would need to find a coach who could top that record.

For Ohio State, the money is only one reason to keep Day, alongside his winning record and a short list of better options.

Alabama would pay one of the steepest prices in college football to fire Kalen DeBoer, but most of that price comes from a promise the school made before its latest move. Firing him would cost Alabama $60.8 million, the third-largest buyout among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. FanSided reports that DeBoer's original contract already ran through 2031, and that Alabama restructured it and added a raise rather than writing a wholly new commitment. Alabama had largely accepted its side of the bill before the new terms. The school's recent changes were aimed at the other side of the contract.

The restructuring set what DeBoer would owe if he chose to leave. Under the original deal, he could have walked away owing Alabama nothing after Jan. 31, 2027, according to FanSided. Michigan and Penn State were rumored to be interested in him, which made a free exit a real risk for the school. The new deal has DeBoer owing $10 million to leave through Jan. 31, 2027, and that gives Alabama some protection. Even so, the contract binds the school far more than the coach. In exchange for a raise, Alabama made DeBoer harder to lure away.

According to recent reports, alabama made this commitment before DeBoer's results could show whether he is the coach for the long run. He has gone 20-8 in his two seasons at Alabama, according to FanSided, and that record has not settled the question. The cost of firing him comes from the terms Alabama wrote, not from how often his teams win. Alabama is paying to avoid starting over, with the expense and risk of a new coaching search at a program that has to keep winning now.

At Alabama, the substantial number is less armor for DeBoer than a premium the school accepted to keep the coach it knows.

Sources indicate that the exact cost of firing Sarkisian is not a single fixed number. The $60.3 million figure dates to Dec. 1, 2025. Longhorns Wire reports a different amount for a firing after the 2026 season, putting the bill at $50.15 million. Even the lower figure would leave Texas paying tens of millions of dollars to a coach it no longer wanted.

Texas now has to decide whether one season's fast fall justifies a check that large.

Few schools have committed to a coach as firmly, or as far into the future, as Clemson has to Dabo Swinney. Firing him would have cost $60 million as of Dec. 1, 2025, the fifth-largest buyout in college football, according to Sports Illustrated, and his salary also ranks among the top 10 in the sport. Clemson pays Swinney like one of the game's elite coaches and has promised to keep doing so for years. Post and Courier reports that his contract runs until 2031, so most of that $60 million covers seasons Swinney has not yet coached. The buyout records how much faith Clemson placed in Swinney when it signed the deal. It does not guarantee his future.

Recent findings suggest that clemson is now weighing that faith against a season that has gone wrong. The team is 6-4 overall and 4-3 in the ACC heading into its game at Duke $DUK, according to Post and Courier, a middling record for a program that has grown used to contending. A school with that record has good reason to ask what a change would cost. At Clemson, the answer is one of the largest bills in college football. A sum that large can make a school hesitate, but it does not take the question off the table. Any decision about Swinney would cost Clemson tens of millions of dollars, and it would be a choice the school makes on purpose.

Clemson made its promise to Swinney before this season, and after a middling year the school now has to decide whether it still wants to keep it.

What outweighed the price was how far the team had fallen from a recent high point. Florida State went 13-0 in 2023, according to The Post and Courier, and that unbeaten season gave fans every reason for faith. The team has gone 10-23 since then and lost far more often than it won. A record that poor over so short a stretch made keeping Norvell harder to defend than paying him to leave. Once losses pile up at that rate, a buyout stops protecting a coach and becomes a cost the school decides to absorb.

It has been revealed that the demand for a change was public before the Clemson game began. Fans at the stadium saw a plane circle overhead towing a banner that read "Fire Mike Novell + Peter Collins," with Norvell's name misspelled. The coach on the other sideline objected to the banner. "Listen, hey, I get it, man. Everybody's got contracts and all this type of stuff, but man, that bothered me," Clemson coach Dabo Swinney noted, as reported by The Post and Courier. Florida State faced that pressure in full view of its own fans and its opponent.

For any school weighing whether to fire a losing coach, Florida State shows that even a huge buyout does not stop a school from acting.

Industry observers note that oregon put one of the steepest prices in college football on its coach while the team was at its best. Firing Dan Lanning would have cost $56.7 million as of December 2025, the seventh-largest buyout among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. Most of that commitment came after Lanning was hired, because his buyout was $20 million when he first signed, according to ESPN reporter Jake Trotter's figures reported by Bleacher Report. The school promised him far more as the team kept winning, and Oregon reached the College Football Playoff semifinals last January. The $56.7 million is a record of what Oregon chose to commit to Lanning while things went right. It does not show how secure he is when they go wrong.

Oregon now has to weigh that price during a slump. The team fell to 4-3 after losing to Illinois, according to Bleacher Report, which is a sharp drop for a program that played in a playoff semifinal months earlier. Oregon outgained Illinois 426 yards to 314 in that game, and the team moved the ball well but could not turn those yards into a win. It also played without its starting quarterback, Dante Moore, who missed a third straight game with a concussion. With Moore out that long, Oregon cannot yet tell whether the coach or the missing quarterback is more to blame for the losses.

In a recent development, lanning has acknowledged that his team is falling short. "I think all things are on the table for us to make sure that we're the best version of ourselves, and we're right now not that. That's very clear," Lanning stated, as reported by Bleacher Report. For now, Oregon would be weighing the $56.7 million against a coach who admits the team is not playing well and a starting quarterback who has missed three straight games.

Industry observers note that the salary gap that put Cignetti in this company has since closed. As of March 2026, he was one of only three active FBS coaches paid $13 million or more a year, along with Georgia's Kirby Smart and Lane Kiffin, according to The Gazette. Indiana once paid him like a mid-tier hire, and it now pays him like one of the sport's elite. The mismatch was a delay rather than a lasting feature of the deal. Indiana wrote the buyout first, and the salary followed.

The $56.7 million measures what Indiana feared losing in late 2025, and the school has paid more to keep him ever since.

It has been revealed that nebraska does not pay Matt Rhule like one of college football's very top coaches, but firing him would cost the school more than almost any other program would pay to replace its coach. His salary ranks only 15th in the sport, yet his $49.6 million buyout is the ninth-largest among football coaches, according to Sports Illustrated. Rhule's contract with Nebraska covered eight years and $74 million in total as of 2023, according to The Associated Press. The length of that promise, not the size of his yearly paycheck, is what places him among the most expensive coaches to fire. The price reveals how long Nebraska pledged to stand by its coach more than how highly it values him in any single season.

Industry observers note that that protection is strongest at the start of the deal and weakens every year the contract runs, whether or not Nebraska does anything. In November 2023, Rhule's buyout stood at $62 million, according to The Associated Press. As of Dec. 1, 2025, Nebraska would have owed him $49.6 million, a much smaller bill only two years later. Any decision about Rhule becomes cheaper for Nebraska the longer the school waits, so the cost of firing him holds the school back less than its size suggests.

Sources indicate that nebraska wrote that protection on purpose. Trev Alberts, the school's athletic director in 2023, considered long terms and buyout clauses the tools that make it harder for a school to push a coach out, according to The Associated Press. He also saw the risk that those tools create for the school itself. "On the other hand, it certainly does put universities in precarious situations if it's apparent a leadership transition is required," Alberts remarked.

At Nebraska, the buyout is a bet that the school will never need to break its promise to Rhule, and each year he stays, Nebraska would pay less if it lost that bet.

Illinois wrote this contract mainly to keep its coach from leaving. Starting July 1, 2026, the school will pay Bielema a retention incentive of $700,000 each year he stays, according to The News-Gazette. "We’ll pay a premium for that kind of certainty for our program and our student-athletes," Josh Whitman, the Illinois athletic director, said. The large firing price is the other side of that premium, because it is what Illinois would owe to give up the certainty it bought.

Bielema's terms are part of a policy that covers much of the Illinois athletic department. The News-Gazette reports that several Illinois coaches have non-compete clauses in their contracts. Whitman notes the school wants steady leaders at a time when college sports treats turnover as normal. Buyouts carry weight in college football because schools replace coaches so often, and Illinois has chosen to spend money to avoid doing the same.

At Illinois, $49.5 million is less a fee for firing Bielema than a measure of how hard the school has worked to make sure it never needs to.

‘We’re begging’: DOGE slashed federal workforce to its lowest in 60 years, and the Trump administration says it still can’t recruit Gen Z workers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.
  • Recent findings suggest that on Nov.
  • It’s a significant problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 12, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor visited Texas Christian University and spoke with students. The reason? Recruiting the next generation of future government workers.

It’s a significant problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor. As of January 2026, young people made up 7.9% of federal employees, down from 8.9% in September 2024 before President Donald Trump took office, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

“I need young, smart people that are coming in, willing to serve,” Duffy said. “You can do it for a lifetime. You can make a career out of it, and that’s wonderful.

According to recent reports, “I find it fascinating that more young people don’t want to apply,” he added. “We’re begging for people to come in.”.

It has been revealed that the administration’s recruiting push has been undercut by an overhaul of the federal workforce when Trump first took office, according to Elizabeth Linos, the Emma Bloomberg Professor of Public Policy and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School. The slashes in headcount, as well as disruptions in workflow as a result of reduced staffing, are discouraging the next generation of talent from joining the federal workforce, she argued, even if DOGE has officially been disbanded for about a year.

According to recent reports, “The government sent a message, in particular to young people, saying these jobs are not going to be safe and they’re not going to be secure,” Linos told Fortune. “Even though there are efforts to try to bring talent into government right now, the administration is basically sending two contradictory messages about whether it wants talent in the federal government to begin with, and I think people hear that conflicting message.”.

Recent findings suggest that OPM debuted the Early Career Talent Network in March, a recruitment push for entry-level workers to apply for finance, human resources, engineering, project management, and procurement jobs within the federal government. The initiative follows the launch of the U.S. Tech Force last December, a hiring initiative for 1,000 engineers and specialists to work with private sector tech companies on the AI buildout within the government.

Industry observers note that the Department of Transportation similarly introduced a campaign in April targeting Gen Z gamers for air traffic controller roles with recruitment videos featuring popular titles like Fortnite. The agency hired more than 2,000 air traffic controllers, breaking the record in October for most air traffic controller trainees hired in a year. The department has more than 4,000 fewer employees total than it did before Trump took office, according to OPM data.

Recent findings suggest that gen Z in particular is struggling in today’s labor market, as the unemployment rate for recent college graduates exceeds that of overall unemployment, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Newly introduced York. With concerns over AI displacement and fewer job opportunities, young people are prioritizing stability and work-life balance, Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found.

According to recent reports, under Elon Musk, DOGE gutted of federal agencies and implemented a deferred resignation program that saw the largest mass resignation in American history last September. Since DOGE’s inception in January 2025, the federal government is more than 258,000 roles smaller, according to Office of Personnel Management data. Even after DOGE was officially disbanded last November, sending its agents to continue their work as employees within the administration’s separate agencies, headcount decreased an additional 42,000 in 2026. About 2.68 million people work for the federal government, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released earlier this month, a decrease of about 1,000 workers from September, and the lowest since summer of 1965.

Recent findings suggest that “By realigning roles, streamlining operations, and modernizing how agencies manage talent, we are strengthening performance and accountability across government,” Kupor noted in a statement to Fortune. “This effort ensures taxpayer dollars support a workforce that delivers efficient, responsive, and high-quality services.”.

Sources indicate that an aging federal workforce has been a problem for years, and is not a result of DOGE or the Trump administration. The U.S. workforce more broadly is aging due to delayed retirement and extended life expectancies, but the government in particular.

The median age of a federal worker is 47 years old, per OPM data, compared to the national average of around 42 years old.

Industry observers note that “We’ve got close to half of our population that’s within 10 years of retirement age,” Kupor told Fortune earlier this year. “So if you just did nothing else, you’ve got this major demographic challenge of a large number of people who will likely either retire or certainly be retirement-eligible over the near term, without us actually replenishing the pipeline of early-career people coming in.”.

According to Linos, DOGE exacerbated the aging of the government workforce by firing primarily probationary employees, or those who had held their positions for a year or less in most cases, many of whom were early in their careers. Court documents show DOGE fired more than 24,000 probationary workers across 18 federal agencies in the first two months of its existence.

The widespread layoffs of early career workers are in tandem with rising discontent among employees who have decided to stay within the federal workforce. The Partnership for Public Service’s Public Service Viewpoint Survey conducted in March found only 7.5% of employees believed their political leaders generated high amounts of motivation in the workforce. OPM officially ended the distribution of the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey, a satisfaction and engagement assessment for federal employees, earlier this month, marking the first time in more than 20 years it will not administer the survey. Instead, individual agencies have the option to distribute their own assessment.

Taken together, Linos explained, the cuts and low morale give young job seekers a reason to look for stable work outside the federal government.

“You could imagine a world where a committed public servant thinks about whether or not the federal government is the place where they can make the biggest impact, and might decide that it’s not anymore in the same way,” Linos remarked. “We’re going to have to rebuild trust in government and in the idea of being able to be a public servant in government over time, and that’s going to take at least a generation. I’m not optimistic about the short-term impacts being reversible.”.

From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary released his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary released his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

In a recent development, the company recently shifted again, adding a new line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary mentioned, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Sources indicate that humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there swiftly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

It has been revealed that I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Newly introduced York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

Recent findings suggest that AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Recent findings suggest that nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

Sources indicate that my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Industry News: Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

In a recent development, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

According to recent reports, the Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any organization planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

In a recent development, the OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

Industry observers note that the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

In a recent development, for existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

Sources indicate that the main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

According to recent reports, on diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

In a recent development, redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

In a recent development, concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

According to recent reports, for an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

It has been revealed that for now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled.
  • Sources indicate that the Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov.
  • On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

Sources indicate that the Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the firm at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

In a recent development, techCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Sources indicate that because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Recent findings suggest that even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the company confirmed in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

Sources indicate that the fund can grow. Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of the company for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company stated it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the tech giant matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to proposal documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

It has been revealed that the third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

The cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

It has been revealed that some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic states it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

In a recent development, the next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

It has been revealed that until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

It has been revealed that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy noted on the tech giant’s earnings call last month.

Amazon declared the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

According to recent reports, decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

In a recent development, decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

In a recent development, the deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

It has been revealed that amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Industry observers note that amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

Industry observers note that the deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other big buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

According to recent reports, “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

Their familiar draw is a bargain in the form of a discounted turkey or a low-priced package of Thanksgiving essentials. Such offers are called loss leaders, meaning that stores charge less than they paid suppliers in hopes of attracting shoppers who will buy other items.

Walmart store workers also mentioned to Business Insider that demand for the Thanksgiving feast is strong.

“The meal deal frenzy has been nuts!” a worker in Oklahoma mentioned. “I work at a neighborhood market, and we are still experiencing a higher volume.”.

It has been revealed that grocery stores are using Thanksgiving as a way to show latest customers what they have on the shelves. Customers come in for the deal and leave with more than they anticipated.

“Thanksgiving is one of the biggest grocery occasions of the year, and it is our chance to show millions of shoppers what we have to offer,” Scott Patton, chief commercial officer at Aldi, said in an interview with the Times.

In a recent development, other grocers are offering more expensive meal bundles. Costco’s $199 Thanksgiving spread included a five-pound precooked turkey breast, accompanied by ready-made mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, apple cobbler and pumpkin pie. Orders closed in mid-November.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Los Angeles luxury grocer Erewhon is taking a pricier approach with its $749 “Ultimate Organic Feast,” which serves up to 10 people. The menu pairs a cooked free-range turkey with sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, garlic mashed potatoes and turkey gravy, along with a deep-dish pumpkin pie.

These prices are outside the norm. Americans will spend $58.63 on average feeding 10 people this Thanksgiving, up 6% annually, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. The increase stems from a 10% increase in turkey prices.

Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some users claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.

The cause the glitch is still unclear, while the reported transactions are yet to be verified.

The incident might have involved thin liquidity problem in Kraken's CAD order books.

Large sell orders reportedly overwhelmed available buy orders, leaving insufficient demand to absorb the selling pressure.

According to some accounts, at one point about 20 BTC was being sold every 15 minutes, causing the imbalance to push BTC price against CAD further down.

It has been revealed that one such transaction resulted in BTC price at around C$24,250, or $16,900. Compared with Bitcoin trading between $57,000-$58,000, the discount amounted to a staggering 71%. Other people reported BTC briefly trading around $27,000.

Kraken's status page continued to show its systems as operational during the incident. No official explanation from the exchange was available at the time of writing.

The reported dislocation highlights the risks associated with trading in markets with limited liquidity. When an order book lacks sufficient buy-side depth, even relatively large sell orders can cause prices to move sharply away from the broader market.

On Friday, Bitcoin price dropped below $60,000. At some point, it fell 5.10% to $55,830, the lowest level since September 2024.

Liquidations on crypto exchanges reached $1.57 billion over 24 hours on Nov. 20.

According to CoinGlass, 265,525 traders were liquidated over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of the total.

In a recent development, bitcoin saw $554.28 million in liquidations, and 91.3% of that amount came from long positions. Ethereum (ETH) fell below $1,700 on Nov. 20, and ETH traders saw $331.08 million in liquidations.

Industry News: Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • According to recent reports, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

According to recent reports, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

In a recent development, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

Sources indicate that the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

According to recent reports, for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

Recent findings suggest that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

Industry observers note that the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

It has been revealed that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

According to recent reports, exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.
